newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam seeks to fix troubled refinery project.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam seeks to fix troubled refinery project.

text.p: Vietnam said on Tuesday it would press ahead with its own feasibility study for the country's first oil refinery, but left the door open for members of a multi-country consortium to remain involved.

The official Vietnam News Agency (VNA) topped weeks of speculation about serious differences between Hanoi and prospective partners with a statement quoting the chief of the state oil firm as saying Vietnam would build the $1.4 billion refinery alone.
"Vietnam will build the nation's first-ever oil refinery at Dung Quat in Quang Ngai province by itself," Petrovietnam's Ngo Thuong San said.
VNA added that Petrovietnam would conduct a new feasibility study for the project which would use capital from official development aid and other sources.
But in a telephone interview later Petrovietnam's board chairman Ho Si Thoang, said the involvement of foreign firms had not been ruled out.
"We did not reject anything or anybody," he told Reuters. "But the project must move forward."

The Dung Quat refinery has had a troubled history from its earliest days. In 1995 French firm Total SA withdrew, branding it economically unviable, chiefly because of its remote location some 1,000 km (600 miles) north of the country's main oilfields.
Indications began emerging in December that not all was well in negotiations between Petrovietnam and the consortium which stepped into Total's shoes to carry out a feasibility study.
The partners are South Korea's LG Group, Stone & Webster Inc, Malaysia's state-owned Petronas, U.S. refiner Conoco, Taiwan's Chinese Petroleum Corp and China Investment Development Corp.
They had sought concessions and additional government-backed incentives to join the project.
But an official with Chinese Petroleum said on Tuesday Vietnam had now formally rejected the bid for favourable terms.
On Monday the company said it was likely to leave the project after calculating it would get at best only half of its expected rate of return on its investment.
Thoang would not comment on the Taiwanese company's statement, but said Petrovietnam had received a letter from LG Group expressing its continued desire to be involved.
He added that if the foreign firms were unwilling to participate directly as partners, possibilities remained for them to be involved in other aspects such as infrastructure construction.
A spokeswoman for South Korea's LG group said LG was still in talks with Petrovietnam to try to convince the firm to stick to its initial deal. She declined to give further comments.
The demise of Dung Quat would represent a major public relations blow for communist Vietnam's foreign investment drive.
Analysts have said the public wrangling between Petrovietnam and the foreign partners may therefore be a negotiating ploy aimed at structuring a final deal to its advantage.
They also point out that Vietnam has neither the capital nor the technology and expertise to mount such an undertaking alone.
Oil industry observers said on Tuesday any move to dump foreign partners and seek funds elsewhere would likely delay the project well beyond the target completion date of 2000.
